reference-frames-s1.title: A moving walkway at an airport
reference-frames-s1.text: An airport walkway 48 m long moves to the right at 1.2 m/s relative to the floor. Ana walks to the right on it at 1.8 m/s relative to the walkway. Ben stands still on the walkway. Cara stands on the floor beside it. Right is positive.
reference-frames-s1.html: Key: orange arrow, the walkway's velocity relative to the floor; gold arrow, Ana's velocity relative to the walkway.

reference-frames-s2.title: Three vehicles on a straight highway
reference-frames-s2.text: A truck, a car and a motorcycle travel along a straight highway. East is positive. The table gives each one's velocity relative to the road.

reference-frames-s3.title: A boat on a river
reference-frames-s3.text: A straight river flows east at 1.5 m/s relative to the bank. A motorboat moves at 4.0 m/s relative to the water. It travels 300 m due east (downstream) between two docks, then returns due west (upstream). East is positive.

items.q: What is Ana's velocity relative to the floor, as Cara measures it?

mistakes.why: Value: 0.60 m/s subtracts the walkway's velocity. Both point right, so they add.

why.correct: Velocity relative to the floor = velocity relative to the walkway + velocity of the walkway relative to the floor = 1.8 m/s + 1.2 m/s = +3.0 m/s.

items.q: How long does Ana take to cover the 48 m walkway?

mistakes.why: Value: 27 s uses only her walking speed. The walkway carries her too, so use 3.0 m/s relative to the floor.

why.correct: Relative to the floor she moves at 3.0 m/s, and the walkway is 48 m long in the floor's frame: t = 48 m ÷ 3.0 m/s = 16 s.

items.q: What is Ana's velocity as Ben measures it?
options: Zero, because they are both on the walkway

why.correct: Ben is at rest relative to the walkway, so in his frame Ana moves at her walking velocity, +1.8 m/s.
options: That is her velocity relative to the floor. Ben is moving with the walkway, not standing on the floor.
That is the walkway's velocity relative to the floor, which Ben shares.
Ben stands still on the walkway while Ana walks on it, so she moves away from him.
Right: Ben moves with the walkway, so he sees only her motion relative to the walkway.

items.q: What is Cara's velocity as Ben measures it?
options: Zero, because Cara is standing still

why.correct: If B moves at +1.2 m/s relative to C, then C moves at −1.2 m/s relative to B. Swapping the observer flips the sign.
options: From Ben's frame, Cara moves the opposite way to how he moves relative to her.
Cara is at rest relative to the floor, not relative to Ben.
Right: Ben moves right at 1.2 m/s relative to the floor, so to him the floor and Cara move left at 1.2 m/s.
That would be relative to Ana. Ben moves only with the walkway, at 1.2 m/s.

items.q: Ana turns around and walks to the left at 1.8 m/s relative to the walkway. What is her velocity relative to the floor?

mistakes.why: Value: −3.0 m/s gives the walkway the wrong sign. It still moves right, +1.2 m/s.
Value: the size is right, but she walks left faster than the walkway carries her right, so her velocity is negative.

why.correct: v(Ana, floor) = v(Ana, walkway) + v(walkway, floor) = (−1.8 m/s) + (+1.2 m/s) = −0.60 m/s: she moves slowly to the left.

items.q: What is the car's velocity relative to the truck?

mistakes.why: Value: 51 m/s adds the velocities. To change frames from the road to the truck, subtract the truck's velocity.
Value: −7.0 m/s is the truck's velocity relative to the car. The car is the faster one, so relative to the truck it moves forward.

why.correct: v(car, truck) = v(car, road) − v(truck, road) = 29 m/s − 22 m/s = +7.0 m/s. From the truck, the car pulls ahead eastward.

items.q: What is the motorcycle's velocity relative to the truck?

mistakes.why: Value: 5.0 m/s adds the truck's velocity. Subtract it: −17 − (+22) = −39 m/s.
Value: the size is right, but the motorcycle moves west relative to the truck, so its velocity is negative.

why.correct: v(moto, truck) = v(moto, road) − v(truck, road) = −17 m/s − 22 m/s = −39 m/s. From the truck, the oncoming motorcycle approaches at 39 m/s.

items.q: Which observer sees the motorcycle moving with the greatest speed?
options: The truck's driver
A person standing at the roadside
The car's driver
Each of the three measures an equal speed

why.correct: Subtract each observer's velocity: road 17 m/s, truck |−17 − 22| = 39 m/s, car |−17 − 29| = 46 m/s.
options: Relative to the truck it is −39 m/s, less than relative to the car, which moves faster toward it.
Relative to the road it is 17 m/s, the smallest of the three.
Right: relative to the car, the motorcycle's velocity is −17 − 29 = −46 m/s, the largest size.
Speed depends on the observer's frame; each observer moves differently.

items.q: The truck's driver brakes, and her velocity relative to the road drops steadily from +22 m/s to +16 m/s in 3.0 s. The car keeps a steady +29 m/s. What is the car's acceleration as measured from the truck?
options: Zero, because the car moves at a steady velocity
+2.0 m/s², because the truck slows while the car does not
−2.0 m/s², the same as the truck's acceleration
+29 m/s², because the car's velocity is 29 m/s

why.correct: Accelerations agree only between frames moving at a constant velocity relative to each other. The braking truck is not such a frame: the car's relative velocity changes by +6.0 m/s in 3.0 s, so +2.0 m/s².
options: Relative to the road the car does not accelerate, but the truck's frame is itself accelerating.
Right: relative to the truck, the car's velocity goes from +7 m/s to +13 m/s in 3.0 s. This frame is accelerating, so accelerations differ.
The truck's acceleration relative to the road is −2.0 m/s²; relative to the truck the car's velocity grows.
A velocity is not an acceleration.

items.q: What is the boat's velocity relative to the bank on the downstream trip?

mistakes.why: Value: going downstream, the current points the same way as the boat, so the velocities add.

why.correct: v(boat, bank) = v(boat, water) + v(water, bank) = +4.0 m/s + 1.5 m/s = +5.5 m/s.

items.q: How long does the upstream return trip take?

mistakes.why: Value: 55 s is the downstream time. Upstream the current works against the boat: 4.0 − 1.5 = 2.5 m/s.
Value: 75 s ignores the current. Relative to the bank the boat moves at 2.5 m/s upstream.

why.correct: Upstream: v(boat, bank) = −4.0 m/s + 1.5 m/s = −2.5 m/s. Time = 300 m ÷ 2.5 m/s = 120 s (two significant figures).

items.q: How does the round-trip time on the river compare with the time for the same 600 m round trip on still water?
options: It is the same, because the current helps one way and hurts the other
It is shorter on the river
It is longer on the river
A comparison needs the mass of the boat

why.correct: Times: river 300/5.5 + 300/2.5 ≈ 55 + 120 = 175 s; still water 600/4.0 = 150 s. Averaging velocities is not averaging times.
options: The help and hurt in speed are equal, but the boat spends more time going slowly, so the effects do not cancel in time.
The downstream gain (55 s instead of 75 s) is smaller than the upstream loss (120 s instead of 75 s).
Right: river 54.5 s + 120 s ≈ 175 s; still water 600 m ÷ 4.0 m/s = 150 s. The slow upstream leg lasts longer than the fast leg saves.
Only velocities and distances are needed.

items.q: A passenger on the boat walks toward the stern (the back) at 1.0 m/s relative to the boat during the downstream trip. What is her velocity relative to the bank?

why.correct: Chain the frames: v(her, bank) = v(her, boat) + v(boat, bank) = −1.0 + 5.5 = +4.5 m/s.
options: Walking toward the stern on an eastbound boat is walking west, so her 1.0 m/s is negative.
Right: v = −1.0 m/s (relative to the boat) + 5.5 m/s (boat relative to bank) = +4.5 m/s.
This leaves out the current: the boat moves at 5.5 m/s relative to the bank, not 4.0 m/s.
That is her velocity relative to the boat only.

items.q: A cart on a flatcar speeds up from rest to 0.60 m/s relative to the flatcar in 2.0 s. The flatcar moves at a constant 5.0 m/s relative to the ground. What is the cart's acceleration relative to the ground?
options: 0.30 m/s², the same as relative to the flatcar
2.8 m/s², because the flatcar's velocity adds 5.0 m/s
Zero, because the cart rides on the flatcar
2.5 m/s², the flatcar's velocity divided by 2.0 s

why.correct: Relative to the ground: v goes from 5.0 to 5.6 m/s in 2.0 s, a = 0.30 m/s². Frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other measure the same acceleration.
options: Right: the flatcar moves at a constant velocity, so adding it changes every velocity by the same amount and leaves Δv unchanged.
A constant added velocity cancels in Δv; it changes velocities, not accelerations.
The cart speeds up relative to the flatcar, so it also speeds up relative to the ground.
The flatcar's velocity does not change, so it contributes no acceleration.

items.q: You sit in a train at rest in a station and see the train beside yours start to move forward. A moment later you realize it is your own train moving backward. Why could you not tell at first?
options: Your train was moving too slowly to have a velocity
The other train had a larger velocity than yours
Motion is visible to a person on the ground, not to a passenger
You saw relative motion, and either train moving looks the same

why.correct: A velocity is measured relative to a reference frame. Seeing only the other train, you measure its velocity relative to your train, which is the same whichever train moves.
options: Any motion is a velocity; the issue is which frame you measure it in.
Neither velocity was larger in a way you could see; you saw only how they moved relative to each other.
Any observer can measure motion; each measures it relative to their own frame.
Right: from your seat, you can only see the other train's motion relative to yours.

items.q: A cyclist rides east at 8.0 m/s relative to the road into a wind blowing west at 5.0 m/s relative to the road. What wind speed does the cyclist feel, relative to herself?

mistakes.why: Value: 3.0 m/s would be the wind she feels if the wind blew east, with her. A headwind and her own motion add.

why.correct: v(wind, cyclist) = v(wind, road) − v(cyclist, road) = −5.0 m/s − 8.0 m/s = −13 m/s. She feels a 13 m/s headwind.
